title: I’m a retired auto dealer who built a stock-picking system. Here are my 5 Month results.
author: Prestigious_Bridge50
selftext:
I spent 35 years in the auto business. Since retiring, I’ve been building an AI stock research system. I now have about five and a half months of testing, starting June 1.

I’d like people who have built or evaluated something similar to pick it apart. I’m keeping the exact methods private, but I can show the results, how many stocks were involved, and where things haven’t gone as well. I’ll call the signals Composite, Signal 1, and Signal 2, and use letters for the portfolios.

# What the replay showed

I tested eight portfolio versions over June 1 through November 11, 2026. The replay summary reports returns ranging from **+9.47% to +17.78%**, with an average of **+15.15%**. SPY rose **0.59%** from the June 1 open to the November 11 close, excluding dividends.

These were broad portfolios. Depending on the version, they held an average of about **40 to 206 stocks at a time**. Across all eight, the replay summary records **2,963 positions opened across 546 different stocks**. That includes repeat purchases and stocks appearing in more than one portfolio.

Here’s the win/loss breakdown at the November 11 cutoff:

* **1,926 positions had closed:** 1,189 were profitable, and 737 lost money or finished flat. That’s a **61.7% closed-position win rate**.
* **1,037 positions were still open:** 686 showed gains, and 351 showed losses or were flat.

Combined, that’s **1,875 positive positions and 1,088 losing or flat**, or **63.3% positive including the open positions**. The open positions covered 297 distinct stocks across the eight portfolios.

There are a few problems in that history I can’t ignore. The portfolio rules were finalized after some of the summer data was already available. Financial inputs before July 10 had a known bug. And June 1 has a timing problem: the signals came out after the market opened, while the replay could buy at that morning’s opening price. I still need to measure what correcting that does to the results.

The replay compounds an average of daily position returns. It isn’t a fixed funded account, and the cost assumptions differ between versions.

# The signals themselves

Separately, I checked the signals against later stock returns.

That study covers signals dated **June 1 through October 19**, using the stored forward-return measure of roughly one month relative to SPY. It includes **21 weekly checks, 26,523 stock-week observations and 1,276 distinct stocks**.

|Signal|Average weekly IC|IC after sector and factor controls|Positive raw-IC weeks|
|:-|:-|:-|:-|
|Composite|0.1440|0.1211|21 of 21|
|Signal 1|0.1335|0.1056|21 of 21|
|Signal 2|0.1739|0.1128|20 of 21|

What interests me is how much of the relationship remains after the controls. Composite’s raw IC was positive in all 21 weekly checks.

Still, the return windows overlap, and many of the same companies appear each week. Twenty-one weekly readings don’t give me 21 independent tests. The earlier financial-input problem applies here too.

# The forward paper record

The eight paper portfolios launched at different times. Their earliest common window is **October 15 through November 18**, covering **25 trading sessions**.

Over that period, recorded returns range from **+0.27% to +4.66%**. The portfolios currently hold between **45 and 219 stocks each**, with **288 distinct stocks** across the eight.

Portfolio A leads that window at **+4.66%**, holding 219 stocks. It closed 46 positions during the period, and 36 were profitable (**78.3%)**. Those are full entry-to-exit results for the positions closed during the window; some were bought earlier.

But take that same portfolio back to its September 3 start and its recorded return is **−0.44%**, with **54 winners and 53 losses among its completed positions**. That’s a **50.5% win rate** over the longer record.

Portfolio A includes 0.10% modeled execution cost per side. Three holdings still use older prices, so the latest result is provisional. The forward books measure daily P&L relative to deployed capital, which differs from the historical replay calculation.

There are also three newer experimental paper books whose first purchases were October 19. They’re down **1.64% to 7.92%** through November 18, and there are gaps in their recorded daily decisions.

# Two honest questions

Looking at the gap between the June–November replays and the noisier forward paper results, what’s the biggest red flag I might be explaining away because I want this to work?

And if the forward results do hold up, where would you see something like this fitting? I won’t put my name on it or charge anyone for it without six to twelve months of forward testing that stands up, with the signals locked before each market open. If it clears that bar, would you keep it for trading your own money, build research software for advisers or institutions, or take it in another direction?

comments.author: Ok_Map5721
comments.body:
the biggest red flag to me is the IC itself. a weekly IC around 0.14 for roughly one-month returns, positive in every check, is much stronger than what usually survives in cross-sectional stock signals. when a signal looks that clean, the first suspect is lookahead: fundamentals stamped with the period date instead of the date they were actually published, the input bug before july 10, or the open-price entry you mentioned. I'd rebuild the study using only data with its real release timestamp and see how much of the 0.14 is left.  
two smaller things: compare the broad portfolios with an equal-weight basket of the same universe, not SPY, since 40–200 names behave very differently from a cap-weighted index. and I'd treat portfolio A from september 3 as the honest number so far, since that's the one picked before seeing the outcome.

replies.author: Prestigious_Bridge50
replies.body:
Thanks, this is the kind of pushback I was hoping for. I went back through the timing, benchmarks, and controls.

The analysis uses scores saved during the period, usually around 4 AM ET. June 1 did come out after the open, so giving that day an opening fill was wrong. What I still can’t provide is a vendor release timestamp for every input. I started hash-sealing the nightly batches on October 14. 

In the latest run, the post–July 10 sample averages 0.156 IC across 15 weekly checks, all positive. The six earlier weeks average 0.108. Excluding the period with the input bug doesn’t weaken the result, although comparing those two periods doesn’t isolate the effect of the fix from the market.

Measuring returns from the next open gives 0.141. Entering a full day later gives 0.139. Dropping the June 1 check gives 0.148.

Your point about controls was useful too. The earlier figure of about 0.12 used a narrower set. Adding sector, size, liquidity, momentum, reversal, volatility, and market beta brings the residual IC down to about 0.06. That’s a substantial reduction. I shouldn’t present the headline number as entirely new stock-selection information.

On the benchmark, the same universe equal-weighted returned about 5% from June 1 to November 11, versus about 0.6% for SPY. The replays still finished ahead, but SPY made the gap look bigger. Correcting the June 1 timing moves the replay average from 15.15% to 15.33%; it doesn’t make the replay an untouched test.

And agreed on Portfolio A: since September 3, it’s at −0.44%. Equal weight lost about 4% over the same dates and SPY about 5.5%, but the t-stat on A’s gap to equal weight is under 1.

Thanks for giving me specific things to check.

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body:
that's a rare reply, most people defend the number instead of cutting it. the timing tests clear the entry, so what's left is the fundamentals timestamps. since you've been hash-sealing nightly batches from october 14, I'd treat that as the real start: residual IC after the same controls, measured only on sealed batches. a few months of that will say more than the whole replay.  
happy to compare notes in DM if you want, I go through the same thing with my own tests.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: The biggest red flag is one you already named. The rules were set after some of the summer data was visible, so the replay isn't a clean test, and the gap between the replay and the forward results is what that usually looks like. Portfolio A going from a good recent window to about flat since its September start also shows how much the window matters. I'd treat only the forward record as real evidence, and I'd compare it with an equal-weight basket of the same stocks, since beating SPY alone can come from the stock universe, not the signals. If you want a tool for the history side, Cymetica's Backtest Labs holds out the last part of the data.

replies.author: Prestigious_Bridge50
replies.body:
Thanks. I agree with your main point. The replay helped me develop the rules, but it isn’t a clean test of whether they work on new data. I’m using the forward record to judge that.

From September 3 through November 18, Portfolio A is at −0.44%. Over the same dates, the equal-weight basket of the same stock list lost about 4% and SPY about 5.5%. Across their own forward windows, all eight books are ahead of equal weight by roughly 3 to 7 percentage points.

I wouldn’t call that proof. The longest record is 54 trading days, the portfolios share many names, and the daily return gaps have t-stats of only about 0.5 to 1.5. Most of the books also lean toward lower-beta stocks, which could explain part of their advantage in a falling market.

You’re right about the window too. A gained 4.66% from October 15 to November 18, while equal weight gained about 1% and SPY lost about 5%. That recent stretch looks much better than A’s roughly flat result since September. The full since-inception record should get the emphasis.

A separate test with daily signals locked before each open began on November 11. I’m planning to follow that through May 2027 and report what happens, including if the advantage disappears.

Thanks for the pointer to Backtest Labs.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
the benchmark is the weak spot. 40 to 206 names is mostly the average stock, and SPY is cap-weighted, so in a year where those came apart the gap can be most of the edge. run the same holding rules on random picks from the same 546 a few hundred times and see where your eight land.

if the 546 came from today's list, names delisted since June are missing too. Quantradin, a free replay desk I built, has that same gap and prints a warning about it. quantradin.com

how did you pick the 546?

replies.author: Prestigious_Bridge50
replies.body:
Thanks. You were right to question the benchmark, so I ran a version of the random-pick test you suggested.

For each of the eight replays, I kept the original entry dates, exit dates, and position sizes, then replaced each stock with a random name from the list scored that day. I ran 300 replacements per portfolio.

The random portfolios averaged about 3% to 5% over the full window, versus about 0.6% for SPY. That shows how much the stock list and trading schedule could produce without my stock selections. The eight replays returned 9.5% to 17.8%, and for each replay, no more than 5 of its 300 random runs did as well or better.

There’s a limitation here: I held the original trade dates fixed. This tests the stock choices given that schedule; it doesn’t rerun the entire strategy with random stocks making their own entry and exit decisions.

It also doesn’t account for choosing the rules after seeing some of the data. The eight portfolios share plenty of names, so I wouldn’t count them as eight independent confirmations. 

For the forward books, a similar comparison with random picks matched on market beta puts them around the 82nd to 99th percentiles, with Portfolio A around the 95th. Those records only cover 16 to 54 trading days. That’s a result worth following, not a probability that the edge is real.

On the 546: that was the number of different stocks traded across the portfolios, not the size of the starting universe. The nightly list had about 1,270 stocks on June 1 and about 1,240 now. It was established in the spring. Roughly 30 names have left, and two were added, with historical membership retained.

Using each day’s list helps make the comparison fairer, but you’re right that I also need to account properly for delistings and missing prices. Keeping a name in the history through its last day doesn’t settle that on its own.

Thanks for the pointer to your replay desk, too.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: that's a real test, and holding the dates fixed is the right first cut since it isolates the picks. 5 of 300 per replay is strong for one run. the shared names are what I'd watch: if the eight lean on the same dozen stocks, it's closer to one confirmation than eight.

comments.author: Prior_Bat5628
comments.body: One gap I’d isolate before interpreting the difference: your replay compounds average position returns, while the paper book reports P&L on deployed capital. For Portfolio A, build a separate daily account-value series for each run with a fixed starting balance, idle cash, positions marked to market, and the same fill-cost assumptions. Then compare the two account series over their shared dates alongside the numbers you already have. With different exposure from day to day, the denominator can explain part of the gap even before you get to the signal.

comments.author: dn4r
comments.body: Sorry if I missed it, but did you factor in fees?
